neighborhood_overview: NorthWest Carrollton, where this apartment is located, is a New Orleans neighborhood bounded by Leonidas Street, Earhart Blvd., Carrollton Avenue and Claiborne Avenue.  We're the “northern” (aka lakeside) peninsula of Carrollton, a historic neighborhood on the National Historic Register.  Craftsman bungalows and raised-basement houses join a mix of early 20th-century house types and styles to define Northwest Carrollton's visual personality. Businesses along Earhart and South Claiborne serve the neighborhood's commercial needs, while Ye Olde College Inn and Rock 'n' Bowl on Carrollton number among the many dining and recreational opportunities. If you aren't sure where Northwest Carrollton is located, just look for the lion statues atop pedestals that herald the entrance to Pritchard Place, developed in 1913.

neighborhood_overview: The spirited Bywater neighborhood is a bit east of the French Quarter and adjacent to the Faubourg Marigny. Bordered by the Mississippi River and new riverfront park on one side and the bustling St. Claude Avenue arts district on the other, the area is a healthy mix of blue collar folks who grew up here, and the more recent bohemian arrivals. Artists and musicians relocated downriver when the French Quarter became too pricey, and the sights and sounds of this historic district reflect that. It is primarily residential but undeniably hip; there are lively pubs, restaurants and randomly placed edgy found-object art scattered throughout the neighborhood. Travelers and residents from other parts of the city are steadily discovering this area's old-time, laid-back charm. The space

neighborhood_overview: The St Roch neighborhood is the new up and coming area of New Orleans, in this neighborhood you can really feel the whole city, it's a melting pot of people! Within less than a quarter mile there is tons more restaurants and bars that are fun and quirky and help to give New Orleans its flair. Or for the traditional route you can take an easy and scenic walk through the Historic Marigny neighborhood and end up on Frenchman Street or the French Quarter in 15 minutes or less! This neighborhood is a real New Orleans neighborhood, there is a lot of art, music, and food right here, but remember that this is a neighborhood and not tourist central (even though all of that is a easy walk to get to). I just want to clarify as it's the only area that I've ever received low(ish) ratings in.

neighborhood_overview: Algiers Point, founded in 1719, largely burned down in 1889, and the rebuilt neighborhood, with its elaborate Victorian architecture, massive oaks, and  grassy parks is a real time capsule. The first plantation owner to do this, Bernard Marigny de Mandeville, owned the land just downriver from Esplanade Avenue.

neighborhood_overview:
The Tremé (pronounced Tre-May) is one of the oldest multi-cultural neighborhoods in the United States and the birthplace of Jazz. The area received its namesake from Claude Tremé, a model hat maker and real estate developer who migrated from Saugivny in Burgundy, France, and settled in New Orleans in 1783.

Tremé continues to be one of the most culturally vibrant neighborhoods in the city, enjoyed by locals and travelers alike. It's central location and proximity to the French Quarter and the Marigny neighborhoods make it an ideal location for visitors seeking to explore the city, especially it's great food and music. Almost every Sunday, you can catch a second-line of people parading with a brass band winding through the neighborhood.

neighborhood_overview:
The French Quarter, also known as the Vieux Carré or the Vieux Carre Historic District, is the oldest section of the city of New Orleans. After New Orleans (La Nouvelle-Orléans in French) was founded in 1718 by Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville, it developed around the Vieux Carré ("Old Square" in English), a central square. The district is more commonly called the French Quarter today, or simply "the Quarter," related to changes in the city with American immigration after the Louisiana Purchase.

Most of the extant historical buildings were constructed in either the late 18th century, during the city's period of Spanish rule, or during the first half of the 19th century, after U.S. annexation and statehood. neighborhood_overview:
The French Quarter, also known as the Vieux Carré or the Vieux Carre Historic District, is the oldest section of the city of New Orleans. After New Orleans (La Nouvelle-Orléans in French) was founded in 1718 by Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville, it developed around the Vieux Carré ("Old Square" in English), a central square. The district is more commonly called the French Quarter today, or simply "the Quarter," related to changes in the city with American immigration after the Louisiana Purchase.

Most of the extant historical buildings were constructed in either the late 18th century, during the city's period of Spanish rule, or during the first half of the 19th century, after U.S. annexation and statehood. The district as a whole has been designated as a National Historic Landmark, with numerous contributing buildings that are separately deemed significant. It is both a prime tourist destination and attractive for local residents.

neighborhood_overview:
The French Quarter, also known as the Vieux Carré or the Vieux Carre Historic District, is the oldest section of the city of New Orleans. After New Orleans (La Nouvelle-Orléans in French) was founded in 1718 by Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville, it developed around the Vieux Carré ("Old Square" in English), a central square. The district is more commonly called the French Quarter today, or simply "the Quarter," related to changes in the city with American immigration after the Louisiana Purchase.

Most of the extant historical buildings were constructed in either the late 18th century, during the city's period of Spanish rule, or during the first half of the 19th century, after U.S. annexation and statehood. The district as a whole has been designated as a National Historic Landmark, with numerous contributing buildings that are separately deemed significant. It is both a prime tourist destination and attractive for local residents.

neighborhood_overview:
The Faubourg Tremé, or as it is more frequently referred to, Tremé, is an ideal, historic neighborhood just steps to the French Quarter.

New Orleans' Tremé neighborhood is geographically the part of the city that lies between North Rampart and North Broad, and from Canal Street to St. Bernard Avenue. The area received its namesake from Claude Tremé, a model hat maker and real estate developer who migrated from Saugivny in Burgundy, France, and settled in New Orleans in 1783. Tremé owned only a small portion of the area that bore his name and was in possession of it for just a decade.

neighborhood_overview:
The French Quarter, also known as the Vieux Carré or the Vieux Carre Historic District, is the oldest section of the city of New Orleans. After New Orleans (La Nouvelle-Orléans in French) was founded in 1718 by Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville, it developed around the Vieux Carré ("Old Square" in English), a central square. The district is more commonly called the French Quarter today, or simply "the Quarter," related to changes in the city with American immigration after the Louisiana Purchase.

Most of the extant historical buildings were constructed in either the late 18th century, during the city's period of Spanish rule, or during the first half of the 19th century, after U.S. annexation and statehood. The district as a whole has been designated as a National Historic Landmark, with numerous contributing buildings that are separately deemed significant. It is both a prime tourist destination and attractive for local residents.

neighborhood_overview:
The French Quarter, also known as the Vieux Carré or the Vieux Carre Historic District, is the oldest section of the city of New Orleans. After New Orleans (La Nouvelle-Orléans in French) was founded in 1718 by Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville, it developed around the Vieux Carré ("Old Square" in English), a central square. The district is more commonly called the French Quarter today, or simply "the Quarter," related to changes in the city with American immigration after the Louisiana Purchase.

Most of the extant historical buildings were constructed in either the late 18th century, during the city's period of Spanish rule, or during the first half of the 19th century, after U.S. annexation and statehood. The district as a whole has been designated as a National Historic Landmark, with numerous contributing buildings that are separately deemed significant. It is both a prime tourist destination and attractive for local residents.

neighborhood_overview:
The French Quarter, also known as the Vieux Carré or the Vieux Carre Historic District, is the oldest section of the city of New Orleans. After New Orleans (La Nouvelle-Orléans in French) was founded in 1718 by Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville, it developed around the Vieux Carré ("Old Square" in English), a central square. The district is more commonly called the French Quarter today, or simply "the Quarter," related to changes in the city with American immigration after the Louisiana Purchase.

Most of the extant historical buildings were constructed in either the late 18th century, during the city's period of Spanish rule, or during the first half of the 19th century, after U.S. annexation and statehood. The district as a whole has been designated as a National Historic Landmark, with numerous contributing buildings that are separately deemed significant. It is both a prime tourist destination and attractive for local residents.

neighborhood_overview:
New Orleans' Tremé neighborhood is geographically the part of the city that lies between North Rampart and North Broad, and from Canal Street to St. Bernard Avenue. The area received its namesake from Claude Tremé, a model hat maker and real estate developer who migrated from Saugivny in Burgundy, France, and settled in New Orleans in 1783. Tremé owned only a small portion of the area that bore his name and was in possession of it for just a decade.

Today, New Orleans' Tremé neighborhood is the locale for visitors and natives alike to celebrate the achievements of African Americans. Various celebrations like second-line parades and jazz funerals are only a few of the lively ways Tremé honors its heritage. Scholars and historians have shared their immense knowledge with New Orleans residents and now Tremé is home to several museums dedicated to African American life, art, and history, as well as Armstrong Park, a memorial to the great jazz legend Louis Armstrong.

Located just minutes away from Treme and The French Quarters. We're called the Esplanade Ridge. The grand address of the Creole upper class in the 19th Century, Esplanade Avenue is a living gallery of 19th and early 20th-century residential architecture. The oak-lined boulevard and surrounding neighborhoods, with proximity to both City Park and Bayou St. John and an excellent stock of historic housing, draw natives and visitors alike to this area.

In 1822 City Surveyor Joseph Pilie mapped the “Esplanade Prolongment” but it would be years before the planned European-style boulevard connecting the Vieux Carre to the bayou would become a reality. Long before the street arrived, however, prominent New Orleanians were building country houses and manor homes along Bayou Road and on large parks dotted across the then-rural area that is now the historic district.

neighborhood_overview:
The French Quarter, also known as the Vieux Carré or the Vieux Carre Historic District, is the oldest section of the city of New Orleans. After New Orleans (La Nouvelle-Orléans in French) was founded in 1718 by Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville, it developed around the Vieux Carré ("Old Square" in English), a central square. The district is more commonly called the French Quarter today, or simply "the Quarter," related to changes in the city with American immigration after the Louisiana Purchase.

Most of the extant historical buildings were constructed in either the late 18th century, during the city's period of Spanish rule, or during the first half of the 19th century, after U.S. annexation and statehood. The district as a whole has been designated as a National Historic Landmark, with numerous contributing buildings that are separately deemed significant. It is both a prime tourist destination and attractive for local residents.

neighborhood_overview:
One of the quietest, most scenic and historic streets in New Orleans, Esplanade Avenue is a hidden treasure running through the heart of the city. From its beginning at the foot of the Mississippi River levee to its terminus at the entrance of City Park, Esplanade is a slow pace thoroughfare with quiet ambiance and local charm.

History

neighborhood_overview:
The neighborhood, which is viewed by many as ground zero of New Orleans culture, seems to be on an upswing as people who have fallen in love with the area's diverse architecture and culture are buying houses to restore. The Historic Faubourg Treme Association has been a force in this renaissance. Among the neighborhood's landmarks are St. Augustine Catholic Church and the Backstreet Cultural Museum, which houses a wealth of Mardi Gras Indian suits.

Although Treme has always been a rich source of African-American culture, it has nurtured a host of black and white New Orleans musicians, including Kermit Ruffins, Shannon Powell, Louis Prima and Alex Chilton. Located at the epicenter of New Orleans culture, the neighborhood also has been home to artists, entrepreneurs, doctors and teachers, and it is being discovered by people in search of the often-elusive combination of affordable prices and architectural elegance.

name: Luxe Resort 1bd apt in Center of French Quarter
description:
This is a full one bedroom unit in The Quarter House Resort. In the middle of the French Quarter!!! Historic brick, plush carpet, luxe finishings... Your own private suite with kitchen, living room, dining table, and daily maid service.

Just off Canal Street, short walk to Bourbon Street, surrounded by foodie paradise. Close enoughto bar hopping paradise to make it home safe on foot, but just far enough not to have your sleep disturbed by it.

The space
Classically furnished. Luxurious feel. The bedroom has no windows--great for sleeping off those 4am finishes in the French Quarter. Flat screen and dvd player in living room and bedroom. There is a full-unit sound system. If you bring your red/white speaker in/3mm plug, you can plug in your phone or iPad and listen in every room--even the bathroom--or control the volume separately in each room. The brick walls generally mean you don't hear your neighbors. I love to spend time at the Quarter House.

name: Nine O Five Royal Hotel, 1 Room Queen Bed
description:
Quaint, European-style inn tucked inside a traditional home hailing from the 1890s, with a shoutout in National Geographic Traveler Magazine as the type of place locals like to house their guests.

The space
This place leans into its historic legacy with a vintage-style sign out front and interiors full of period furnishings – think four-poster beds, vintage phones, floral lamps and patterned wall coverings. If you book a suite, have a seat on the balcony and watch the horse-drawn carriages clip by out front, or find a quieter spot in the courtyard. Look for the tongue-in-cheek plaque outside noting ‘Rip Van Winkle slept here.’

neighborhood_overview:
Known for its colorful street murals, the Bywater neighborhood has a bohemian vibe, with plenty of outdoor cafes, boisterous dive bars and hip restaurants. Quirky boutiques selling handmade goods dot the area, while buzzy St. Roch Market offers southern gourmet specialities in a stylishly updated Victorian food hall. Trails, picnic spots and sweeping city views are the draw at riverside Crescent Park.

A vibrant art scene - with local artisans' galleries, funky live music venues, and art markets, embodies the essence of these adjacent neighborhoods. The food scene here is mixed with trendy spots and locally founded, casual digs - take your pick. Explore the St. Claude Arts District, Crescent Park on the riverfront, and more.

The area was originally developed between 1832 and 1900 and is considered one of the best-preserved collections of historic mansions in the Southern United States. The 19th-century origins of the Garden District illustrate wealthy newcomers building opulent structures based upon the prosperity of New Orleans in that era.

This whole area was once a number of plantations, including the Livaudais Plantation. It was sold off in parcels to mainly wealthy Americans who did not want to live in the French Quarter with the Creoles. It became a part of the city of Lafayette in 1833, and was annexed by New Orleans in 1852. The district was laid out by New Orleans architect, planner, and surveyor Barthelemy Lafon.

A few minutes walk to the street car, Frenchman Street (10 mins), and the French Quarter (15 min), our home is located in an ideal neighborhood to stay in while visiting New Orleans.

If you stay here, we're sure you'll love our artsy, somewhat bohemian neighborhood. Our neighborhood is very walkable, has ample (delicious) restaurants and bars, parks, grocery stores etc all very nearby.

We maintain our home in clean, cozy, and welcoming state as our reviews reflect.

The space
The space you will rent is a private bedroom within a historic New Orleans home built in 1888 (our primary home). This will also include access to a shared bathroom (which we commit to keep very clean during your stay!).

Like many homes in the Marigny, our home is nondescript from the outside, but surprisingly expansive once you enter! It is full of historic details and charm - and we hope you enjoy our interior design which is one of our chief passions.

North of the noise and saturated color of the Quarter is a New Orleans neighborhood that’s perfected the art of living. “Welcome to Mid-City,” read the signs on the neutral ground. And that’s truth in advertising. It’s the kind of place where your auto mechanic invites you to a crawfish boil and a total stranger may buy you a drink at an Irish pub or a cannoli at an Italian bakery. Take the red streetcar line up Canal to the Cemeteries (Mid-City’s dead neighbors are as interesting as the live ones) or bike the new 2.6-mile-long Lafitte Greenway that stretches from Basin Street to Carrollton Avenue and, conveniently, past a po’ boy shop or two – or 17 – with a sno-ball shop and a micro-brewery thrown in for good measure. Buttermilk biscuits. Live music. A bowl of Vietnamese pho. Who wouldn’t want to visit? Eat. Drink. Get up here.

neighborhood_overview: North of the noise and saturated color of the Quarter is a New Orleans neighborhood that’s perfected the art of living. “Welcome to Mid-City,” read the signs on the neutral ground. And that’s truth in advertising. It’s the kind of place where an auto mechanic invites you to a crawfish boil and a total stranger may buy you a drink at an Irish pub or a cannoli at an Italian bakery. Take the red streetcar line up Canal to the Cemeteries (Mid-City’s dead neighbors are as interesting as the live ones) or bike the new 2.6-mile-long Lafitte Greenway that stretches from Basin Street to Carrollton Avenue and, conveniently, past a po’ boy shop or two – or 17 – with a sno-ball shop and a micro-brewery thrown in for good measure. Buttermilk biscuits. Live music. A bowl of Vietnamese pho. Who wouldn’t want to visit? Eat. Drink. Get up here.

neighborhood_overview:
Mid-City is a neighborhood that has carved out its own unique identity. It is a generally local, middle-class neighborhood in that it contains fewer tourist destinations than other parts of the city. Restaurants and bars rely heavily on local clientele, giving the area a quirky local flavor.

A sub-district of the Mid-City District Area, Mid-City's boundaries as defined by the City Planning Commission are: City Park Avenue, Toulouse Street, North Carrollton and Orleans Avenues, Bayou St. John and St. Louis Street to the north, North Broad Street to the east, and the Pontchartrain Expressway to the west. It is a historic district on the National Register of Historic Places. Colloquially, a somewhat larger area surrounding these borders is often also referred to as part of Mid-City.

neighborhood_overview:
Algiers Point offers a rich mix of history, architecture and small town charm only minutes away from the world famous French Quarter. Enjoy a short walk to the peaceful ferry, on the way you'll pass historic creole cottages, shotgun doubles and majestic Victorians and take in the best view of the city from the Mississippi river levee.

The Point is home to locally owned and operated restaurants, cafes, bars, pubs and a blown glass studio, all located in buildings dating back to 1800's. Algiers Point takes its name from nautical maps that identify the bend in the river as it curves around the neighborhood. Algiers Point was placed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1978 and designated a local historic district in 1994.

A few or our neighborhood favorites (all less than a 10 minute walk):

-Faubourg Fresh Market (small grocery store with all the necessities & some local specialties)
-Crown & Anchor English Pub (traditional English pub)

name: Sonder | The Printing Press | One-Bedroom Apartment w/ Balcony
description:
Amidst reimagined historic warehouse spaces of industrial New Orleans, a stroll from the lively magic of Canal Street, and in the bustling Central Business District — welcome to The Printing Press. Although in the middle of NOLA, this stretch of Girod Street provides a soothing rest from the bustle of the Big Easy. Soak up some Louisiana sunlight through floor-to-ceiling windows in your space, where muted tones of the furnishings and tilework are complemented by artistic pops of color. We love the ethos of Pluck winebar on the ground floor: to serve better wine for everyone. Begin your evening with a glass of pinot noir to experience the meaning for yourself. Just around the corner, enjoy some live entertainment at the friendly green space of Lafayette Square. Or hop between the museums and galleries of the area for a sample of Southern history and contemporary art.

The space

neighborhood_overview: Anchored by restored theaters and new arenas, like the Orpheum and Mercedes-Benz Superdome, each street of the Central Business District promises unforgettable experiences with glittery lights and spectacular libations. Once referred to as the “downtown” of New Orleans, this historic city center now balances 19th-century architecture with sleek new high rises, housing an array of new restaurants and retail stores. After shopping along Canal Street or in the South Market District, savor the delectable Southern eateries found on each street corner, featuring Cajun-Creole favorites and mouthwatering seafood delicacies. As the sun begins to set over the Bayou, grab a cocktail and enjoy the live jazz and blues spilling from the doorways of some of New Orleans' most popular bars and nightclubs.

neighborhood_overview:
The house is located in the Mid City neighborhood of New Orleans which is just about as centrally located as you can get. Pretty much anything in the city is a 5-10 minute Uber ride and the Canal Street Streetcar line is only five blocks away. There are plenty of great restaurants and bars located in Mid City and the surrounding areas, some within walking distance. Although largely off the tourist radar, Central City has long been an important thread in the city's cultural tapestry. This is one of the city's major African American neighborhoods, and a major focal point for Second Line and Mardi Gras Indian culture. Heroes of the Civil Rights movement fought their battles for social justice in these streets, and today, Central City serves as another sort of staging ground: a jumping off point for revitalization of urban blight. Up-and-coming Central City is a working class area known for its Mardi Gras parades and unpretentious Cajun eateries. Exhibits, performances and film screenings at Ashé Cultural Arts Center celebrate African-American culture, while the Southern Food & Beverage Museum has displays on regional gastronomy and hosts tasting events. The New Orleans Jazz Market is a sleek modern venue for concerts and cocktails.

The Lower Garden District is famous for its parks, restaurants, and history!

The area was originally developed between 1832 and 1900 and is considered one of the best-preserved collections of historic mansions in the Southern United States. The 19th-century origins of the Garden District illustrate wealthy newcomers building opulent structures based upon the prosperity of New Orleans in that era.

This whole area was once a number of plantations, including the Livaudais Plantation. It was sold off in parcels to mainly wealthy Americans who did not want to live in the French Quarter with the Creoles. It became a part of the city of Lafayette in 1833, and was annexed by New Orleans in 1852. The district was laid out by New Orleans architect, planner, and surveyor Barthelemy Lafon.

name: Private & Authentic Bourbon Street Maisonette
description:
Surround yourself with history and antiques in vieux Nouvelle-Orléans at our one-of-a-kind creole maisonette, which is the only surviving one in the French Quarter. Many people often believe the structure is a servant’s quarters, however it was the original structure on the property before a double was built in front of it. Circa 1824 and nearly original, this is how New Orleans is meant to be lived in...

The space
Our two story maisonette has a parlor, dining room, and kitchen on the main floor. Upstairs there is a large, principal bedroom (with a closet), a smaller secondary bedroom, and a full bath with a tub/shower. Everything inside and out is "of the period" (18th & 19th century) with a few modern exceptions. You will have television in the main bedroom and wifi throughout. Often called the Crown Jewel of New Orleans, the French Quarter is one of NOLA's most historic neighborhoods. But you'll find plenty of new mixed in with the old. There’s a reimagined French Market, modern boutiques and artisan cocktails mix with beloved antique stores and old restaurants. (Antoine’s. Arnaud’s. Galatoire’s. Brennan’s – the world would be far less flavorful without you!)

Like the Creole aristocrats lining the galleries of the Historic New Orleans Collection, the French Quarter is a timeless portrait – especially come dusk when swallows glide above the fortunetellers on Jackson Square and St. Louis Cathedral’s butter-crème-colored walls reflect the fiery sunset. neighborhood_overview: Anchored by restored theaters and new arenas, like the Orpheum and Mercedes-Benz Superdome, each street of the Central Business District promises unforgettable experiences with glittery lights and spectacular libations. Once referred to as the “downtown” of New Orleans, this historic city center now balances 19th-century architecture with sleek new high rises, housing an array of new restaurants and retail stores. Mid City is an awesome part of town. I am right up the street from all the businesses on Banks st- pizza, breakfast restaurants, bank st bar and around the corner from Mid City Yacht Club.

I walk/bike to City Park all the time and highly recommend it.

The Lafitte Greenway starts close by and is a quick 10 minute bike ride to the French Quarter/Marigny/Bywater. On Mondays there is a Farmers Market on the Greenway and if you ride your bike there, you get a $2 token to spend at the market.

name: Family home | blocks to Tremé, FQ, Frenchmen
description:
**20RSTR-30852 + 20RSTR-30849**

Welcome to our home! We are a young family of three, and we live in the downstairs unit of this duplex, although you're unlikely to see us during your stay since the entrances to each unit are on opposite ends of the building. Please understand house rules before booking and we look forward to hosting you,

The space
**For groups of more than 8 people: please note that two of the bedrooms contain only a full bed with twin trundle (pull-out twin) underneath. So while these bedrooms can technically accommodate two guests, they become rather cramped when trundle is in use. See last two photos for better visualization.**

This building's layout is a bit unconventional: officially a duplex, but functionally a triplex. We live in the downstairs/front unit, which features a guest suite to the rear, referred to as Bedroom 5 of this listing. This suite boasts its own (rear) outside entrance, bathroom, kitchenette, t
neighborhood_overview:
We moved to this corner of the 7th Ward in 2016, and it's a hodgepodge, which suits us. Mixed race, mixed income, stray cats, stray chickens, stray people. Colorful historic Creole cottages next to manufactured homes next to dilapidated structures and vacant lots next to pricey new construction/renovation. Families, artists, shift workers, porch sitters, teachers, healthcare workers... plenty of potholes.

Perhaps more compelling to visitors will be our proximity to higher-profile neighborhoods you've probably heard of: Tremé, French Quarter, Marigny, all are blocks away.

A quick note: we have browsed many guest reviews of other Airbnbs in the immediate vicinity, and it's not uncommon to see our neighborhood referred to as "sketchy" or "feeling unsafe." You should be able to view our home's specific location on the map in this listing, so I encourage you to embark on a virtual tour via Google StreetView and get a feel for yourself.

neighborhood_overview: Although largely off the tourist radar, Central City has long been an important thread in the city's cultural tapestry. Heroes of the Civil Rights movement fought their battles for social justice in these streets. Up-and-coming Central City is a working class area known for its unpretentious Cajun eateries. Exhibits, performances and film screenings at Ashé Cultural Arts Center celebrate African-American culture, while the Southern Food & Beverage Museum has displays on regional gastronomy and hosts tasting events. The New Orleans Jazz Market is a sleek modern venue for concerts and cocktails.

The neighborhood, which is viewed by many as ground zero of New Orleans culture, seems to be on an upswing as people who have fallen in love with the area's diverse architecture and culture are buying houses to restore. The Historic Faubourg Treme Association has been a force in this renaissance. Among the neighborhood's landmarks are St. Augustine Catholic Church and the Backstreet Cultural Museum, which houses a wealth of Mardi Gras Indian suits.

Although Treme has always been a rich source of African-American culture, it has nurtured a host of black and white New Orleans musicians, including Kermit Ruffins, Shannon Powell, Louis Prima and Alex Chilton. Located at the epicenter of New Orleans culture, the neighborhood also has been home to artists, entrepreneurs, doctors and teachers, and it is being discovered by people in search of the often-elusive combination of affordable prices and architectural elegance.

neighborhood_overview:
North of the noise and saturated color of the Quarter is a New Orleans neighborhood that’s perfected the art of living. “Welcome to Mid-City,” read the signs on the neutral ground. It’s the kind of place where your auto mechanic invites you to a crawfish boil and a total stranger may buy you a drink at an Irish pub or a cannoli at an Italian bakery. Take the red streetcar line up Canal to the Cemeteries (Mid-City’s dead neighbors are as interesting as the live ones) or bike the new 2.6-mile-long Lafitte Greenway that stretches from Basin Street to Carrollton Avenue and, conveniently, past a po’ boy shop or two – or 17 – with a sno-ball shop and a micro-brewery thrown in for good measure. Early in the city's history, it was the main neighborhood of free people of color, and remains an important center of the city's African-American and Creole culture, especially the modern brass band tradition.

The modern Tremé neighborhood began as the Morand Plantation and two forts—St. Ferdinand and St. John. Near the end of the 18th century, Claude Tremé purchased the land from the original plantation owner. Developers began building subdivisions throughout the area to house a diverse population that included Caucasians, Haitian Creoles, and free pe of color.

Although largely off the tourist radar, Central City has long been an important thread in the city's cultural tapestry. This is one of the city's major African American neighborhoods, and a major focal point for Second Line and Mardi Gras Indian culture. Heroes of the Civil Rights movement fought their battles for social justice in these streets, and today, Central City serves as another sort of staging ground: a jumping off point for revitalization of urban blight. Up-and-coming Central City is a working class area known for its Mardi Gras parades and unpretentious Cajun eateries. Exhibits, performances and film screenings at Ashé Cultural Arts Center celebrate African-American culture, while the Southern Food & Beverage Museum has displays on regional gastronomy and hosts tasting events. The New Orleans Jazz Market is a sleek modern venue for concerts and cocktails.

neighborhood_overview: North of the noise and saturated color of the Quarter is a New Orleans neighborhood that’s perfected the art of living. “Welcome to Mid-City,” read the signs on the neutral ground. And that’s truth in advertising. It’s the kind of place where your auto mechanic invites you to a crawfish boil and a total stranger may buy you a drink at an Irish pub or a cannoli at an Italian bakery. Take the red streetcar line up Canal to the Cemeteries (Mid-City’s dead neighbors are as interesting as the live ones) or bike the new 2.6-mile-long Lafitte Greenway that stretches from Basin Street to Carrollton Avenue and, conveniently, past a po’ boy shop or two – or 17 – with a sno-ball shop and a micro-brewery thrown in for good measure. Buttermilk biscuits. Live music. A bowl of Vietnamese pho. Who wouldn’t want to visit? Eat. Drink. Get up here.

The area was then bought by the New Orleans Canal and Banking Company and was divided into sections. neighborhood_overview:
Today, New Orleans' Tremé neighborhood is the locale for visitors and natives alike to celebrate the achievements of African Americans. Various celebrations like second-line parades and jazz funerals are only a few of the lively ways Tremé honors its heritage. Scholars and historians have shared their immense knowledge with New Orleans residents and now Tremé is home to several museums dedicated to African American life, art, and history, as well as Armstrong Park, a memorial to the great jazz legend Louis Armstrong.

New Orleans' Tremé neighborhood is geographically the part of the city that lies between North Rampart and North Broad, and from Canal Street to St. Bernard Avenue. The area received its namesake from Claude Tremé, a model hat maker and real estate developer who migrated from Saugivny in Burgundy, France, and settled in New Orleans in 1783. Tremé owned only a small portion of the area that bore his name and was in possession of it for just a decade.

And that’s truth in advertising. It’s the kind of place where your auto mechanic invites you to a crawfish boil and a total stranger may buy you a drink at an Irish pub or a cannoli at an Italian bakery. Take the red streetcar line up Canal to the Cemeteries (Mid-City’s dead neighbors are as interesting as the live ones) or bike the new 2.6-mile-long Lafitte Greenway that stretches from Basin Street to Carrollton Avenue and, conveniently, past a po’ boy shop or two – or 17 – with a sno-ball shop and a micro-brewery thrown in for good measure.
